capabilities.target: Arbitrary external URL supplied by the model

inputs.source: Employee question via SSO-authenticated chat channel
Engineering design docs, retrieved via docs.search (write-restricted to engineers)
Jira tickets surfaced by a planned Jira MCP server, including tickets filed by customers

instructions.note: The only control against disclosing sensitive material is a prompt rule ('never paste secrets or credentials'). It is purely behavioral, is scoped narrowly to literal secrets/credentials rather than confidential content generally, and has no structural backstop such as output scanning or redaction.

controls.name: Prompt rule: never paste secrets or credentials into answers
controls.decay_rationale: Relies on the model choosing to obey a narrow instruction. It is scoped to literal secrets/credentials, not confidential design-doc content generally, and it only examines the visible chat reply text, not arguments passed to other tools such as a future web.fetch call. A more capable or adversarially prompted model can rationalize exceptions or route sensitive content through a channel the rule never inspects.

controls.name: Chat client does not render images or fetch links in replies
No network egress capability exists today
Destination allowlist for web.fetch (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed or implemented. If built to exclude attacker-writable destinations, it would sever the exfiltration path; the roadmap note gives no indication such an allowlist is planned.

controls.name: Untrusted-content tagging / injection classifier for Jira ticket content (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Not yet designed. Even if built, a classifier that inspects content rather than intent can be bypassed by multi-turn or encoded payloads, and it weakens further as new sources (new_mcp_server) and stronger models (model_upgrade) are introduced.

controls.name: Raw-action human approval before any web.fetch call to a non-allowlisted domain (recommended)

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1), forecast only: customer-filed Jira content + confidential doc read + new web.fetch egress

attack_path.note: A customer-filed Jira ticket (planned source, untrusted) enters the agent's context once the Jira MCP server is connected. Nothing in the design tags this content as untrusted.
The agent reads confidential engineering design docs under a shared read-only credential while handling the (possibly injected) request.

The agent is induced to call the new web.fetch tool with a URL whose query string embeds confidential doc content, sending it to an attacker-controlled destination. No egress allowlist or approval gate is declared for this tool.

forecast.watch_signal: Tool manifest diff adding a 'web.fetch' entry, or MCP client config diff adding a Jira MCP server connection; also watch for any indexing of ticket content into the agent's retrieval or reasoning context.

evidence.observation: The team plans to add a web.fetch tool and a Jira MCP server that includes tickets filed by customers; neither addition is described with any accompanying egress, input-trust, or approval control.

The only safety instruction ('never paste secrets or credentials into answers') is scoped to literal secrets/credentials in the visible chat reply and does not cover confidential design-doc content embedded in a web.fetch tool-call argument.

evidence.locator: runtime notes: 'There is no network egress today. The credential is read only.'
evidence.observation: Today's architecture has no egress capability at all, which is the structural fact currently preventing this pattern from being exploitable. The new_tool trigger (adding web.fetch) removes exactly this fact.

recommendations.action: Before deploying web.fetch, enforce a destination allowlist limited to approved reference domains and block arbitrary or user-writable destinations.
Tag all Jira ticket content, especially customer-filed tickets, as untrusted input and apply spotlighting or an injection classifier before it can influence tool-call arguments.
Require raw-action human approval (full URL and payload visible, not a summary) before any web.fetch call to a non-allowlisted domain, at least until the allowlist is proven effective.
Log all web.fetch destination URLs and alert when query parameters resemble document identifiers or content fragments.

rating.rationale: The present design has no complete attack path at moderate risk or higher: docs.search uses a read-only credential, there is no network egress capability of any kind, and replies go only to the same authenticated employee who asked (the chat client also does not render images or fetch links, closing the classic reply-channel exfiltration trick). Inherent and residual are therefore both low today, with no present-horizon findings filed. The roadmap, however, adds two elements that together complete a lethal trifecta (TC1): a Jira MCP server surfacing customer-filed (untrusted) ticket content, and a web.fetch tool that gives the agent its first egress path. No control is declared or planned to cover this combination -- the one prompt rule in place is scoped to literal secrets/credentials and does not inspect tool-call arguments, and the structural fact that currently blocks exfiltration (no egress capability) is exactly what the new_tool trigger removes. The forecast is rated critical because, absent new controls, an untrusted source reading confidential data and egressing it is an unmitigated S3 path the moment both roadmap items ship. The single highest-leverage fix is a destination allowlist on web.fetch (ctl.egress_allowlist), paired with treating Jira ticket content as untrusted input before it can shape tool-call arguments.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration described in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior.

No MCP configuration, tool manifest, or IaC was provided; the docs.search and chat_reply capabilities are inferred from a short prompt and narrative runtime notes, and the planned web.fetch tool and Jira MCP server are inferred from a single roadmap sentence with no interface or control details, so their modeling is necessarily approximate.

The exact mechanism by which Jira ticket content would enter the agent's reasoning (direct indexing versus only when a user pastes a ticket link) is undocumented; the attack path assumes ticket content becomes reachable by the agent once the server is connected.
